title: A quarter of the universe’s ordinary matter is helium made in its first few minutes
body: On 9 September 2026 a team using the Large Binocular Telescope published the most precise measurement yet of the universe’s first helium: **24.58%** of ordinary matter by mass, pinned down to about 0.5% by studying 15 small, distant galaxies whose stars have barely changed their original gas ([Ohio State](https://news.osu.edu/using-helium-astronomers-blow-certainty-into-early-big-bang-conditions/)). The recipe behind that number is short. About a second after the Big Bang there was roughly one neutron for every six protons. Free neutrons decay, half of them in about 10 minutes, and no nuclei could last until the universe was cool enough for deuterium to survive the light. By then about one neutron was left per seven protons, and almost all of them ended up in helium-4, two neutrons and two protons each: 4 particles out of every 16, a quarter of the mass. Worked through in full, with the density of matter measured by the Planck satellite, the recipe predicts 24.67%, which [agrees with the measurement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.22238).

slides.question: Of every 100 kg of ordinary matter that came out of the Big Bang, about how many kilograms were helium?
slides.explanation: About 25 kg, and almost all the rest hydrogen. A 2026 measurement puts helium at 24.58% of the mass, give or take about 0.13 points.

slides.alt: Animation of the young universe as a glowing soup: neutrons in blue and protons in coral, one per six. Two neutrons decay, light breaks up deuterium, then 7 helium nuclei form from 28 of 112 particles. Then pristine galaxies, their spectra and the 2026 value, 24.58%, against the predicted 24.67%.

slides.prompt: Slide the moment the first nuclei can form. When does the universe end up with the 24.6% helium measured in 2026?
slides.takeaway: About 2.2 minutes in this simplest model. Wait 10 minutes and half the neutrons have decayed, leaving about 14% helium. Full calculations follow every reaction and predict 24.67%.

slides.heading: How the Big Bang made helium

steps.label: One second in: 1 neutron per 6 protons
Free neutrons decay, half in about 10 min
Cool enough: deuterium survives the light
Nearly every neutron ends up in helium-4

slides.heading: Why pristine galaxies
slides.text: Stars make helium too, along with heavier elements such as oxygen, so the less of those a galaxy’s gas holds, the closer its helium is to the original mix. The team measured more than 10 helium lines and 15 hydrogen lines in the glowing gas of each galaxy, in 130 hours of observing.

slides.question: Why couldn’t the first nuclei form straight away after the Big Bang?
slides.explanation: Until the universe cooled, light smashed every deuterium nucleus, the first step towards helium. Meanwhile free neutrons kept decaying, so the wait set how much helium was made.

source.label: Aver et al., The LBT Yp Project IV: A New Value of the Primordial Helium Abundance (arXiv, 2026)
